📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Deep learning models are constrained by hardware. Memory limits batch size and model size; compute limits training throughput. Optimization techniques — quantization, pruning, distillation, efficient architectures — can shrink models 10x with minor accuracy loss. Essential when deploying to phones, edge devices, or scaling inference.

Core concepts

1. The cost dimensions. Training cost: GPU-hours to train. Inference compute: FLOPs per prediction. Memory footprint: model weights + activations. Each can dominate. Mobile deployment cares about memory and inference latency; cloud training cares about GPU-hours.

2. Quantization — lower precision. Convert weights from 32-bit floats to 8-bit integers (or 4-bit). 4x memory reduction; often faster inference. Modern quantization (post-training quantization, quantization-aware training) recovers most accuracy. Standard for production deployment of deep models.

3. Pruning — remove weights. Many trained weights are near zero and contribute little. Pruning sets them to exactly zero, enabling compressed storage and (on supporting hardware) faster inference. Magnitude pruning, structured pruning, lottery ticket hypothesis. 50-90% sparsity often possible with small accuracy loss.

4. Knowledge distillation. Train a small student model to mimic a larger teacher model's output distribution. Student matches much of the teacher's accuracy with a fraction of the parameters. Used for BERT → DistilBERT, GPT-3 → smaller variants, and almost every production deep learning system.

5. Efficient architectures. MobileNet, EfficientNet, MobileBERT, TinyML architectures. Designed for mobile/edge deployment from the ground up rather than starting big and shrinking. Often the cleanest path to small models.

6. Mixed precision training. FP16 or BF16 instead of FP32 for forward/backward pass. About 2x speedup on modern GPUs. Standard for serious training runs. Requires loss scaling for FP16 (BF16 doesn't). Framework support is mature.

7. Inference optimization stacks. ONNX Runtime, TensorRT, OpenVINO, Core ML. Compile a trained model for specific hardware. Operator fusion, kernel optimization, hardware-specific tricks. Usually 2-5x speedup over generic Python inference. Always run a model through one before claiming production-ready.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Skipping quantization for production models — leaving 4x memory and significant latency on the table.
  • Pruning aggressively without retraining — accuracy crashes.
  • Distilling without enough student-teacher overlap data — the student doesn't mimic well.
  • Reporting research-paper speeds when production requires inference optimization stacks.

Quick recap

Compute and memory optimization shrinks models for deployment. Quantization (FP32 → INT8) gives 4x memory reduction and faster inference. Pruning removes near-zero weights. Distillation trains compact students from large teachers. Efficient architectures are designed small from the start. Mixed precision speeds training. Inference compilers (TensorRT, ONNX Runtime) optimize for production.

Glossary

Quantization
Reducing numeric precision (e.g., FP32 → INT8) for smaller, faster models.
Pruning
Removing low-magnitude weights to compress and speed up models.
Knowledge distillation
Training a small student model to mimic a large teacher.
Mixed precision training
Using lower-precision floats during training to speed up computation.
Inference compiler
Tool optimizing a trained model for specific hardware (TensorRT, ONNX Runtime).

Data parallelism: copy the SAME model to each GPU and feed each a different shard of data — gradients are combined. Model parallelism: the model itself is SPLIT across GPUs because it cannot fit on one. And caching predictions for repeated inputs avoids recomputation entirely — the cheapest inference is the one you never run.

📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section

📖 Worked example — shipping the model as an API

WORKED EXAMPLE — churn model to production, the path
1. Serialize the trained model (pickle/joblib/ONNX).
2. Wrap in an API: a Flask/FastAPI endpoint — POST /predict with customer features → {churn_prob: 0.83}.
3. Containerize (Docker) so the environment travels with the code; deploy behind a load balancer or as serverless.
4. Modes: real-time API (per-request, low latency) vs batch scoring (nightly job scores everyone — simpler, fine for weekly retention campaigns). Edge deployment puts the model on-device.
5. Versioning + rollback: every model artifact versioned; a bad deploy rolls back like any software release.
Match the mode to the decision cadence — the exam scenario names it (instant fraud check → real-time; monthly mailer → batch).
⚠️ TRAINING ENV ≠ SERVING ENV
Feature computation must be IDENTICAL in both (same code path if possible) — training-serving skew is the deployment bug that quietly ruins live accuracy.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

A model in a Jupyter notebook is not a product. Deployment is the bridge from training to serving real predictions in real time to real users. The work is largely software engineering — APIs, scaling, monitoring, versioning — but with ML-specific concerns. Production deployment is where most ML projects either ship or stall.

Core concepts

1. Deployment patterns. Batch: precompute predictions on a schedule. Online API: serve predictions on request. Embedded: run on-device (mobile, edge). Streaming: process events as they arrive. Each pattern has different latency, throughput, and operational characteristics. Pick by use case, not by familiarity.

2. Online APIs and model servers. REST or gRPC service wrapping the model. Tools: TensorFlow Serving, TorchServe, Triton, BentoML, Seldon, custom Flask/FastAPI. Standard production pattern. Add auth, rate limiting, request validation, structured logging.

3. Containerization. Package model + dependencies in a Docker container. Reproducible across environments. Deploy to Kubernetes, AWS ECS, Cloud Run, etc. Image size matters — slim base images plus optimized model weights make for faster cold starts.

4. Model versioning. Multiple versions in production simultaneously: old version handles legacy traffic, new version handles canary traffic. Version model artifacts, training data, code. MLflow, DVC, model registries. When something breaks, roll back to a known good version.

5. A/B testing and canary deployment. Don't replace v1 with v2 instantly. Route 5% of traffic to v2, monitor metrics, expand gradually. Detect regressions before they hit everyone. Online metrics may differ from offline metrics; the test catches what offline missed.

6. Edge and on-device deployment. Mobile (Core ML, TFLite), browsers (TensorFlow.js, ONNX Runtime Web), embedded (TFLite Micro). Tighter constraints; quantized small models. Privacy benefits — data doesn't leave device. Update mechanism is harder than for cloud models.

7. Serverless deployment. AWS Lambda, Cloud Functions, Vercel. Scales to zero when idle. Cold starts can hurt latency for large models. Best for low-volume or sporadic workloads; container/Kubernetes for sustained high volume.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Deploying without versioning — when something breaks, you can't tell what changed.
  • Pushing v2 to 100% traffic instantly — regressions become incidents.
  • Forgetting to optimize the model for inference (quantization, ONNX) before deployment — leaving performance on the table.
  • Not implementing logging and monitoring — production failures are invisible until users complain.

Quick recap

Deployment patterns: batch, online API, embedded, streaming. Containerization for reproducibility. Versioning for rollback. Canary deployment for safety. Edge deployment for privacy and offline. Serverless for sporadic loads. The work is largely software engineering with ML-specific monitoring and rollback discipline.

Glossary

Model serving
Running a trained model to produce predictions in production.
Containerization
Packaging model and dependencies in a Docker container for portable deployment.
Model versioning
Tracking and managing multiple versions of trained models.
Canary deployment
Routing a small fraction of traffic to a new version to detect regressions.
Edge deployment
Running models on user devices rather than cloud servers.

Serving options: FastAPI — the modern Python API framework (async, type hints, auto-generated docs); Flask — the simple, minimal Python web framework; and managed cloud ML platforms — AWS SageMaker, GCP Vertex AI, Azure ML — which handle hosting, scaling, and monitoring for you at higher cost.

📊 FIGURE — how this section fits together

📖 Worked example — a predictive-analytics project, end to end

WORKED EXAMPLE — forecasting next month’s demand
1. Question: units per product next month (regression/time-series).
2. Features: lagged sales (1/3/12 months), seasonality flags, promotions, price.
3. Model + honest eval: gradient boosting; TIME-based split (train ≤ March, test April) — random splits leak the future.
4. Numbers → decisions: forecast 1,200 ± 150 units → order stock, staff shifts. The analytics ladder: descriptive (what happened) → predictive (what will) → prescriptive (what to DO about it).
5. Feedback loop: compare forecast vs actual monthly; retrain on schedule.
The graded distinction: prediction is only valuable when wired to a DECISION with costs attached.
⚠️ TIME DATA SPLITS BY TIME
Random CV on time-series lets the model peek at the future — offline glory, production faceplant. Forward-chaining evaluation is the required answer.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Predictive analytics is the discipline of using historical data and statistical/ML models to forecast future events. Demand forecasting, customer churn, lead scoring, predictive maintenance, fraud detection — the applications are vast. The mechanics build on supervised learning; the business value depends on framing and integration.

Core concepts

1. The predictive workflow. Define the prediction target (what specifically to forecast). Gather historical data with the target observed. Engineer features available at prediction time. Train a model. Evaluate on held-out data. Deploy. Monitor. Same as any supervised ML, with extra emphasis on what's available WHEN.

2. Time as the central axis. Predictive analytics predicts future from past. Strict temporal discipline: features available before prediction time, target observed after. Train/test splits respect time. Without this, models look amazing offline and fail in production.

3. Common applications. Customer churn (will user X churn in 30 days). Demand forecasting (units of product Y next quarter). Predictive maintenance (will machine Z fail). Lead scoring (probability of conversion). Each has decades of accumulated wisdom about features and pitfalls.

4. Forecasting horizons. Short-term (hours to days): real-time data dominates. Medium (weeks to months): seasonality and trend matter. Long (years): more uncertain; conditional forecasts more useful than point estimates. Different methods fit different horizons.

5. Confidence intervals matter. A point prediction without uncertainty is half useful. 'Demand will be 1000 units' versus 'demand will be 800-1200 with 80% confidence' enable different decisions. Quantile regression, conformal prediction, Bayesian methods all give intervals. Use them when downstream decisions are risk-sensitive.

6. Drift kills production models. Customer behavior changes. New product categories appear. Economic conditions shift. Models trained on yesterday's data degrade against tomorrow's. Continuous monitoring and periodic retraining are not optional features — they're the core of production predictive analytics.

7. From prediction to decision. A model that predicts 'this customer will churn' is just information. The value comes from action: contact them with an offer, route them to retention. Closing the prediction-to-action loop is most of what makes predictive analytics economically valuable. ML teams that don't measure downstream action effectiveness leave money on the table.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Predictions that don't drive decisions — pretty dashboards, no business impact.
  • Time-leaking features — model uses information not available at prediction time; production fails.
  • Point predictions without uncertainty — downstream decisions can't account for risk.
  • Deploying once and forgetting — drift makes accuracy decay silently.

Quick recap

Predictive analytics forecasts future events from historical data. Strict temporal discipline. Common applications include churn, demand, maintenance, lead scoring. Forecasting horizons drive method choice. Provide confidence intervals when decisions are risk-sensitive. Monitor for drift; retrain periodically. Close the loop from prediction to action — the business value is in decisions, not predictions.

Glossary

Predictive analytics
Discipline of using historical data to forecast future events via statistical or ML models.
Forecasting horizon
Time period into the future the prediction covers.
Confidence interval
Range expressing uncertainty around a point prediction.
Concept drift
Change in the underlying data distribution over time, degrading model accuracy.
Conformal prediction
Framework providing prediction intervals with statistical guarantees.

📘 Deep dive: time series & forecasting

A time series is a sequence of observations ordered in time (daily sales, hourly temperature). Classic decomposition splits it into trend (long-run direction), seasonality (repeating cycles), and residual noise. Prophet — the open-source forecasting library from Facebook/Meta — fits trend + seasonality + holidays and is a strong default for business series. Rule: never randomly shuffle time-series data for train/test splits — always split by time, training on the past to predict the future.

Forecast numbers never speak for themselves — interpretation requires domain knowledge: a demand spike may be a holiday, a promotion, or a data error, and only context tells you which.

📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section

📖 Worked example — adapting a model to a new domain

WORKED EXAMPLE — reuse, don’t retrain from scratch
You have an image model trained on 1M product photos; the new task is classifying 2,000 furniture photos.
Transfer learning: keep the pretrained network’s early layers (edges/textures generalize), replace the final layer, fine-tune on the 2,000 — matching or beating a from-scratch model at 1% of the cost. Same pattern powers NLP: pretrain on the internet, fine-tune on your tickets.
When domains differ more (X-rays, not photos): fine-tune deeper layers, or collect more target data. Watch for domain shift: evaluate on the NEW domain’s own test set, never assume the old metrics carry over.
⚠️ SMALL DATA + RELATED DOMAIN = TRANSFER LEARNING
That phrase pattern in a question points to transfer learning/fine-tuning every time; training from scratch on 2,000 images is the trap option.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Trained models are valuable assets. Reusing them for related problems — through transfer learning, fine-tuning, prompting — multiplies their value. Knowing when and how to adapt rather than train from scratch is one of the highest-leverage skills in modern ML.

Core concepts

1. Transfer learning — the broad idea. Take a model trained on one task; adapt it for another related task. Most modern ML — especially NLP and vision — works this way. Foundation models (BERT, GPT, ResNet) are explicitly designed to be transferred. Training from scratch is the exception, not the rule.

2. Fine-tuning. Continue training a pretrained model on your specific dataset. Update some or all weights. Requires labeled task-specific data (much less than training from scratch). Standard for adapting BERT to your classification problem, ResNet to your image domain, etc.

3. Feature extraction. Use a pretrained model's intermediate layers as feature extractors; train a small task-specific head on top. Keeps the bulk of the model frozen. Faster, less data needed, lower risk of catastrophic forgetting. Sometimes outperforms full fine-tuning when target data is small.

4. Few-shot and zero-shot with LLMs. LLMs can perform new tasks from a few examples in the prompt (few-shot) or just instructions (zero-shot). No training. Useful for prototyping, low-data tasks, and tasks that change frequently. Quality varies by task; sometimes a tiny fine-tuned model beats a much larger prompted one.

5. Prompt engineering. Crafting prompts that elicit better LLM behavior. System prompts, few-shot examples, chain-of-thought scaffolding, output structure constraints. The new 'feature engineering' for LLM-based systems. Iterative; reproducibility requires version-controlled prompts.

6. LoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning. Update only a small number of parameters (low-rank adapters) instead of all weights. Order-of-magnitude memory savings; trainable on consumer GPUs. Standard for fine-tuning large LLMs. Adapter swaps let one base model serve many specialized tasks.

7. When to adapt vs train. Adapt when: similar task, smaller dataset, time/compute constrained, foundation models exist for the domain. Train from scratch when: no relevant pretrained models exist, your task is fundamentally different, you have massive data and compute. The bias today is heavily toward adapting.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Training from scratch when fine-tuning a foundation model would work in 1% the time.
  • Fine-tuning all weights with too little data — catastrophic forgetting wipes out pretrained knowledge.
  • Treating prompt engineering as a one-shot — prompts need iteration, evaluation, and version control.
  • Underestimating LoRA — it works very well and democratizes fine-tuning of large models.

Quick recap

Transfer learning reuses pretrained models for new tasks. Fine-tuning continues training on target data. Feature extraction freezes most weights. Few-shot and zero-shot prompting bypass training entirely. LoRA enables parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large models. Adapt rather than train from scratch as the default; train from scratch only when adaptation isn't viable.

Glossary

Transfer learning
Reusing a model trained on one task for a different but related task.
Fine-tuning
Continuing training of a pretrained model on task-specific data.
Feature extraction
Using a pretrained model's hidden layers as fixed features for a new task.
Few-shot learning
Performing a new task from a few examples without explicit training.
LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation)
Parameter-efficient fine-tuning method updating only small adapter matrices.

📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section

📖 Worked example — monitoring a live model & catching drift

WORKED EXAMPLE — the model that rotted quietly
Churn model shipped in January at F1 0.81. Monitoring dashboards track:
• Input/data drift: feature distributions shift (a new pricing plan appears the model never saw).
• Prediction drift: flag-rate creeps from 8% to 15%.
• Performance: as true labels arrive (who actually churned), live F1 = 0.64 by June → concept drift — the world changed, the mapping changed.
Response: alert thresholds → investigate → retrain on recent data (scheduled or trigger-based) → A/B the new model before full rollout. Plus operational health (latency, errors) and fairness metrics by group, continuously — models are perishable.
⚠️ DEPLOYMENT IS THE MIDPOINT, NOT THE END
“What happens after deployment?” → monitor drift + performance, retrain on schedule/trigger, version and roll back. Any option ending at “deploy” is incomplete.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Models in production decay. Distribution shifts, label drift, upstream data pipeline changes, simple bugs — all silently degrade performance. Without monitoring, you discover problems when users complain. With monitoring, you fix them before users notice. ML maintenance is most of the work after deployment.

Core concepts

1. What to monitor. Input data: distribution shifts, missing values, schema changes, volume. Predictions: distribution shifts, confidence levels, rare-class predictions. Performance: accuracy, latency, error rates by slice. Business outcomes: did the model improve the actual KPI? Each layer reveals different problems.

2. Data drift detection. Compare current input distribution to training distribution. Statistical tests (KS, chi-square), distribution-distance metrics (Jensen-Shannon, PSI), or simpler thresholds on summary statistics. Drift doesn't always mean degraded performance, but it's a strong signal to investigate.

3. Performance monitoring requires labels. Without ground truth, you can't compute accuracy. For some problems, labels arrive eventually (delayed): churn confirmed after 30 days, fraud confirmed after investigation. For others, labels never arrive automatically — sample manual labeling needed.

4. Slicing in production. Overall performance can be fine while a subgroup degrades. Monitor metrics per important slice (geography, customer segment, product category). The same fairness slicing from development carries into production monitoring.

5. Alerting and on-call. Alerts on what matters: performance below threshold, latency spike, error rate climb, drift detected. Avoid alert fatigue — only alert on things requiring human action. Have on-call rotation for ML systems just like for software systems. Document runbooks.

6. Retraining cadence. Some models retrain daily; others quarterly. Drives: how fast the world changes, how expensive retraining is, how harmful drift is. Triggered retraining (when drift exceeds threshold) plus scheduled retraining (insurance) is common. Automate the pipeline; manual retraining is brittle.

7. Shadow mode and challenger models. Run a new model in shadow alongside the current one — compare predictions, don't act on shadow. Validates new model on real production data before promotion. Challenger models compete; pick winner based on metrics. Standard for de-risking model updates.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Monitoring only aggregate metrics — slice-level degradation hides.
  • Alerting on noisy thresholds — alert fatigue desensitizes the team.
  • No retraining cadence — drift accumulates silently.
  • Promoting new models without shadow validation — surprises hit production users.

Quick recap

Production ML requires monitoring at every layer: input data, predictions, performance, business outcomes. Detect drift via statistical tests. Track metrics by slice. Have alerts and on-call. Retrain on a cadence and on triggers. Use shadow mode for de-risking new models. Maintenance is ongoing, not optional — it's most of the work after deployment.

Glossary

Data drift
Change in input distribution between training and production.
Concept drift
Change in the relationship between inputs and target.
Slice metric
Performance metric computed on a specific subgroup (geography, segment, etc.).
Shadow deployment
Running a candidate model alongside the current one without acting on its predictions.
Challenger model
Candidate model competing against the production model on production data.

Rollback: when a new model misbehaves in production, revert to the previous version immediately — keep old versions deployable. A feature store centralizes feature management so training and serving compute features the SAME way. MLOps is DevOps applied to the ML lifecycle — versioning, CI/CD, monitoring for data and models, not just code.

Metaheuristics: genetic algorithms & simulated annealing

📊 FIGURE — the steps, in order
💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

For huge, bumpy search spaces where exact optimization is infeasible, metaheuristics are clever guided-search strategies that find good (not always perfect) solutions. Their trick is escaping local optima — spots that look best only compared to their immediate neighbors.

⚙️ WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

Genetic algorithm (GA): keep a population of candidate solutions. Each generation: score them with a fitness function, select the fitter ones, combine pairs via crossover, apply random mutation, and repeat. Over generations, solutions evolve toward higher fitness.

Simulated annealing (SA): explore from a single solution, sometimes accepting worse moves to escape local optima. The willingness to accept worse moves is controlled by a temperature that cools over time — lots of exploration early, fine-tuning late.

GA VOCABULARY
TermMeaning
PopulationSet of candidate solutions
FitnessHow good a candidate is (objective value)
SelectionPrefer fitter candidates to reproduce
CrossoverCombine two parents into offspring
MutationRandom tweak that maintains diversity
ESCAPING LOCAL OPTIMA
Plain hill-climbing gets stuck at the first peak it finds. GAs escape via population diversity + mutation; SA escapes by sometimes accepting worse solutions (probability high when temperature is high, shrinking as it cools).
📝 EXAM WORDING

Metaheuristics find near-optimal solutions in large spaces and escape local optima. GA cycle: fitness → selection → crossover → mutation over a population. SA accepts worse moves with a probability set by temperature, which follows a cooling schedule. Mutation preserves diversity; too little → premature convergence.

🎯 OA-STYLE CHECK
What lets simulated annealing escape a local optimum?
  1. It always moves downhill
  2. It sometimes accepts worse solutions, more often when temperature is high
  3. It uses a population
  4. It never accepts worse moves
Show answer
B. SA probabilistically accepts worse moves — likely when hot, rarely when cool — so it can climb out of local optima before settling.

📖 Worked example — mapping an AI-project PA to deliverables

WORKED EXAMPLE — one requirement, one artifact, every time
AI-project PAs ask you to propose/build a solution for a scenario. Translate requirements to artifacts:
• “Describe the business problem and AI approach” → the framing spec (decision, task type, metric, baseline) from ch1.
• “Prepare the data” → data dictionary + cleaning steps + the split strategy (and WHY stratified/time-based).
• “Develop and evaluate the model” → training code/notebook + confusion matrix + precision/recall/F1 with interpretation.
• “Optimize” → before/after table: baseline vs tuned (what you changed, what improved).
• “Deployment/monitoring plan” → serving mode + drift/retraining plan.
Work the list in order — each artifact feeds the next, and each maps to a rubric aspect one-to-one.

The deliverable in one picture

D682 is a project, not a multiple-choice exam. You are given a scenario and asked to implement an AI/ML solution in Python, evaluate it honestly, and then optimize it so you can show a measurable before/after gain. You submit three things: (1) your code (usually a notebook or scripts), (2) a written report that walks an evaluator through your reasoning and results, and often (3) a short video demonstrating the running solution. Confirm the exact deliverables and task wording in your own course shell, since WGU adjusts these over time.

The typical task flow

  1. Frame the problem & select an approach. Decide whether the scenario is classification, regression, clustering, or optimization, and justify the algorithm family you pick against that framing.
  2. Prepare the data. Handle missing values and outliers, encode categoricals, and scale features. Do a proper train/test split and fit any transformer (scaler, encoder, imputer) on the training data only.
  3. Implement a baseline model. Get an honest first result you can improve on.
  4. Evaluate. Use metrics that match the task: accuracy/precision/recall/F1 (and confusion matrix) for classification; RMSE/MAE/R² for regression. Discuss under- and over-fitting using train-vs-test gaps.
  5. Optimize. Tune hyperparameters (grid or random search), add regularization, or apply a metaheuristic (genetic algorithm, simulated annealing, PSO). Report the same metric before and after so the gain is visible.
  6. Document reproducibility. Pin a random seed, list library versions, and give clear run instructions.

What evaluators reward

Every claim must be supported by an output in the code. "I optimized the model" is only credible if a printed metric moved. Keep your narrative and your numbers in lockstep.

📖 Worked example — an AI-PA rubric aspect, graded

WORKED EXAMPLE — “evaluates the model appropriately”
Not evident: “the model achieved 97% accuracy.” (Imbalanced data — accuracy alone is the known trap.)
Approaching: reports precision/recall but doesn’t interpret them.
Competent: confusion matrix + metric CHOICE justified by the scenario’s costs (“missed churners cost more than wasted offers, so recall is primary”) + honest limitations (“test set is one quarter; drift risk noted”).
The pattern for every technical aspect: show the artifact, justify the choice with the scenario, state the limitation. Screenshots/outputs beat claims.

Passing every aspect on the first submission

D682 is scored against a competency rubric. Exact aspect IDs and point values change over time, so confirm the wording in your course; the competencies below are stable. The evaluators grade evidence in your code, not intentions in your prose.

CompetencyWhat evaluators look forHow to nail it
Problem framing & approach selectionA clear statement of the task type and a justified algorithm choiceName the problem (classification/regression/etc.), then explain why your chosen model fits the data and goal
Data preparationCleaning, encoding, scaling, and a correct train/test split with no leakageSplit first, then fit the scaler/encoder on train only and transform both; document every step
Implementation correctnessCode that runs end-to-end and produces the reported outputsRestart-and-run-all before submitting; make sure every number in the report is reproduced by the code
Evaluation with correct metricsTask-appropriate metrics and a discussion of fitClassification: accuracy, precision, recall, F1, confusion matrix. Regression: RMSE, MAE, R². Compare train vs. test to diagnose over/under-fitting
Optimization & demonstrated improvementA tuning/metaheuristic method plus a measurable gainPrint the same metric before and after; use grid/random search, regularization, or a GA/SA/PSO and report both scores
Documentation, reproducibility & ethicsSeeds, versions, run steps, and a discussion of bias/limitationsSet random_state, list library versions, give run instructions, and address data ethics and model limits

The evaluator's mindset

Aspects are graded independently, so a strong model with a leaky split still fails the data-preparation aspect. Treat each competency as its own checklist item and provide explicit, locatable evidence for each one.

📖 Worked example — pre-submit sweep for an AI PA

WORKED EXAMPLE — a returned submission, diagnosed
Case: returned on “data preparation” — the notebook cleaned data, but the WRITTEN report never explained what was cleaned or why. Code isn’t self-explaining to a grader reading the report.
Fix: a data-prep section: issues found (missing values in 12% of tenure, 40 duplicates), action taken (median imputation, dedup), and why — mirroring the notebook.

The sweep: every requirement verb → labeled section; every technical claim → visible artifact (output, matrix, chart); metric choice justified against the scenario; splits/leakage addressed explicitly; limitations stated; files run top-to-bottom in a fresh environment; submission list checked against the task page.

Pre-submission build checklist

  • Split before you transform. Call train_test_split first, then scaler.fit(X_train) and scaler.transform(X_test). Fitting on the full set is the classic data leakage return reason.
  • Right metric for the task. Do not report accuracy on a regression, or R² on a classifier. On imbalanced classes, emphasize precision/recall/F1 over raw accuracy.
  • Real improvement. Optimization must move a number. Show baseline vs. optimized side by side; if the metric did not improve, tune further or explain honestly rather than claiming a gain that the output does not show.
  • Claims match results. Every sentence in the report that states a number should be traceable to a cell output. Remove any assertion the code does not back up.
  • Reproducible. Set random_state everywhere randomness enters (split, model, search, metaheuristic), list versions, and do a clean Restart & Run All.

Why PAs get returned

Return reasonFix
Data leakage (scaler fit on full data before split)Split first; fit transformers on train only
No measurable improvement from "optimization"Report before/after on the same metric; keep tuning until a real gain shows
Wrong metric for the taskClassification → accuracy/precision/recall/F1; regression → RMSE/MAE/R²
Claims not supported by resultsTie every stated number to a code output; delete unsupported claims
Non-reproducible codePin seeds, list versions, provide run steps, and re-run from a clean kernel

Metaheuristics done right

If you use a genetic algorithm, simulated annealing, or PSO to optimize hyperparameters or feature subsets, define the fitness function as your validation metric, seed the random generator, and compare the metaheuristic's best result against your baseline and against a standard grid/random search so the benefit is clear.

🧠 The Aistote Method (J-Method)

THE IDEA
The Aistote app is built on two of the most evidence-backed study techniques — active recall and spaced repetition — run in short, intense 25-minute blocks (its "J-Method"). Instead of slowly re-reading, you spend the time testing yourself and re-testing what you miss. This app already has every tool the method needs.
THE 3-STEP LOOP
StepWhat you doWhere in this app
1. ConvertTurn the material into questions instead of re-reading it.Open a section, skim the lesson once, then jump to its Quiz.
2. RecallAnswer from memory first — no peeking — then check.Take the section Quiz, or a PA / OA simulation; rate your confidence.
3. Space itRe-test only what you missed, on a growing schedule.Every miss becomes a Flashcard; review them on the app's spaced-repetition schedule.
A 25-MINUTE J-METHOD SESSION
TimeDo this
0–3 minSkim the lesson's key terms and the big idea — don't memorize yet, just get the lay of the land.
3–18 minTake the section quiz (or a 15-question drill). Try to recall the answer first, reveal it after.
18–23 minRedo only the questions you got wrong.
23–25 minSend the stubborn ones to Flashcards and note tomorrow's quick review.
Start the block with the ⚡ Focus timer (25 min) on any lesson — that is your J-Method session.
⚠️ THE ONE RULE
Always try to answer from memory before you look. The effort of retrieving is what actually builds the memory — re-reading feels productive but barely moves it.
WHY IT WORKS
Active recall (testing yourself) forces your brain to reconstruct the answer, which strengthens it far more than recognition. Spaced repetition reviews each fact just as you're about to forget it, moving it into long-term memory with the fewest reps. The 25-minute block simply makes you actually do both, every day.
DAILY RHYTHM
Two or three 25-minute J-Method blocks a day (new material in one, missed-question review in the next) beats a single long cram session — and it's how the Aistote method delivers "learn it in 25 minutes" instead of hours.

Framing AI Problems

Data Sources and Collection

Core concepts — 1. What features are. Features are the inputs the model sees. Raw fields can be features but rarely are best. Date column → day of week, month, hour. Address → distance…

📋 Model Evaluation and Testing

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

Evaluation Metrics

⚠ ACCURACY LIES ON IMBALANCED DATA The single most-tested fact in the course. When classes are skewed, report precision/recall/F1 (or AUC) — never accuracy alone.

Cross-Validation

⚠ CV REPLACES THE VALIDATION SPLIT, NOT THE TEST SET With 5-fold CV, do you still need a test set? → yes, for the untouched final evaluation. And k=5 or 10 is the conventional answer to choose k.

Bias-Variance Tradeoff

Core concepts — 1. Decomposing prediction error. Total error = bias² + variance + irreducible noise. Bias: how far the model's average prediction is from truth. Variance: how much the…

Quick recap — Bias is being too simple; variance is fitting too much to training data. Total error is bias² + variance + noise. Diagnose by comparing training and validation error.…

Glossary

Error Analysis and Debugging

⚠ GAP PATTERN → DIAGNOSIS Train high + val low = overfit. Both low = underfit. Both high offline, bad in production = leakage or drift. This three-row table answers most what s wrong with this model? questions.

"},"D682/cheat/c5":{"body":"

📋 Optimization Techniques

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

Algorithmic Optimization

⚠ SYMPTOMS OF A BAD LEARNING RATE Loss exploding/NaN → too high. Loss barely moving → too low. Loss plateauing then dropping with a schedule → rate decay working. Matching symptom to cause is the exam form.

Regularization

⚠ L1 SPARSIFIES, L2 SHRINKS Which produces sparse models / selects features? → L1. Which smoothly shrinks all coefficients? → L2. Two-word answers to the most repeated question in the unit.

Ensemble Methods

⚠ PARALLEL vs SEQUENTIAL IS THE TELL Independent models trained in parallel on bootstrap samples → bagging. Each model corrects its predecessor → boosting. The exam phrases it exactly this way.

Compute and Memory Optimization

Core concepts — 1. The cost dimensions. Training cost: GPU-hours to train. Inference compute: FLOPs per prediction. Memory footprint: model weights + activations. Each can dominate.…

Quick recap — Compute and memory optimization shrinks models for deployment. Quantization (FP32 → INT8) gives 4x memory reduction and faster inference. Pruning removes near-zero…

Glossary — Data parallelism: copy the SAME model to each GPU and feed each a different shard of data — gradients are combined. Model parallelism: the model itself is SPLIT across GPUs because it doesn't fit on one — layers or tensor shards distributed. Data parallelism scales throughput; model parallelism enables size.

📋 Deployment and Predictive Analytics

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

Model Deployment

⚠ TRAINING ENV ≠ SERVING ENV Feature computation must be IDENTICAL in both (same code path if possible) — training-serving skew is the deployment bug that quietly ruins live accuracy.

Predictive Analytics

⚠ TIME DATA SPLITS BY TIME Random CV on time-series lets the model peek at the future — offline glory, production faceplant. Forward-chaining evaluation is the required answer.

Adapting Models to New Applications

⚠ SMALL DATA + RELATED DOMAIN = TRANSFER LEARNING That phrase pattern in a question points to transfer learning/fine-tuning every time; training from scratch on 2,000 images is the trap option.

Monitoring and Maintenance

⚠ DEPLOYMENT IS THE MIDPOINT, NOT THE END What happens after deployment? → monitor drift + performance, retrain on schedule/trigger, version and roll back. Any option ending at deploy is incomplete.
